This research expands upon that framework by exploring a similar combination of lambda calculus and the semantics of quantificational formulas within first-order logic.  A corresponding lambda term is proposed for each valid instantiation of quantificational formulas, such that applying this term to the same variables as the original formula results in a lambda term that behaves identically to the original quantificational formula for all possible combinations of argument values.  A key aspect of this research is demonstrating that every possible quantificational formula is equivalent to a lambda term satisfying this condition using a specific, combinatory expression consisting of a limited set of basic lambda terms, which in turn is shown to be computationally enumerable.  Ultimately, this research demonstrates the efficacy of this approach by exemplifying the methodology using simple existential and universal sentences, as well as more complex expressions.  A key aspect of this research is also the identification of its limitations, which include the recognition that neither the strategy employed nor the results achieved provide a solution to the general problem of quantificational formulas being expressible through lambda calculus.  Nevertheless, the research offers a novel, innovative solution for a substantial subset of first-order logic, which in turn paves the way for further exploration of this problem's other components.  A key contribution of this research is the development of a novel algorithm that translates valid instantiations of quantificational formulas into corresponding lambda terms, fueling potential applications of the resulting expressions in the field of computational biology.   In epidemiological research, understanding age-specific rates of incidence (AI) and prevalence (AP) is crucial, as these rates vary significantly across different age groups. AI represents the probability of new cases occurring within a given time frame in a specific age group, whereas AP signifies the probability of existing cases present in that age group at a particular moment. 
  Historically, separate methods have been employed for estimating AI and AP. Nonetheless, given the interconnected nature of these quantities, there's a growing interest in modeling them jointly. 
  This work reviews recent publications on shared-space models, with a focus on models utilizing continuous-time data. We begin by examining models where AI and AP are modeled independently but share the same time-varying covariates. 
  Subsequently, we investigate models where both AI and AP are modeled as functions of the same set of time-vary meta-process parameters. This has given rise to novel computational challenges, resolvable with the aid of recent Bayesian methods. 
  We then outline the results of applying these models to simulated data sets and real-world data, featuring the Pooled COVID-19 Infection Survey (PCIS) conducted in South Korea. 
  Ultimately, our aim is to enhance knowledge of AI and AP modeling, as well as promote the use of such modeling in future studies.

Alternative approaches use unlabelled images and machine learning methods to infer object locations automatically, but these methods are highly prone to errors.  A key technique employed by top performing models is the utilization of contrastive learning, which draws upon the premise that similar data samples ought to have similar latent representations.  However, applying contrastive learning solely to images isn't sufficient to leverage its full potential for object detection.  A novel approach is presented here, which employs a two-tiered strategy combining two contrastive learning techniques - one focused on visual features and the other on semantic attributes of objects. Evaluations conducted on the COCO dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior accuracy to other unlabelled object detection methods, matching the performance of methods utilizing labeled data. Moreover, our research sheds light on the relationship between null controllability, exact controllability, and stabilization in a class of semilinear equations. Our goal is to determine Josephson current properties of this type of junction, particularly when the unconventional superconductor is in the form of a mesoscopic triangle with the s wave superconductor and itself sharing p wave boundary components.  Firstly, we analyze a conventional scenario in which the unconventional superconductor forms a narrow strip connected to a s wave superconductor, demonstrating that the mesoscopic effect has a minimal impact on the average pairing symmetry.  However, when the width of this strip is comparable to the superconducting coherence length, the mesoscopic effect becomes significant, resulting in oscillations in the critical current and corresponding interference patterns.  Secondly, we investigate the mesoscopic triangular mesostructure, which exhibits more intricate behavior, giving rise to multiple possible pairing modes and corresponding interference patterns, and we compare these to corresponding results from a narrow superconducting strip.  Our study indicates that the mesoscopic triangular structure supports a robust mode associated with the combination of s and d waves, in contrast to narrow strips where this mode is highly fragile and subject to breakdown at relatively low ratios of width to coherence length. This paper focuses on an associated yet distinct task, Information Retrieval (IR) within the same framework. Our goal is to develop an automated ranking system that can efficiently identify the most relevant documents containing the topic words specified in the test topics. This study employs Supervised Learning techniques, combining traditional features derived from document and topic characteristics with modern Neural Network-based Document Embedding features. We further investigated an innovative approach, which incorporates Neural Network-based Document Embedding features in a supervised learning framework. This allowed us to replace the initial $k$-means clustering with a Hierarchical Clustering algorithm, which effectively reduced the topic detection system's latency. We experimented with different traditional features and Neural Network-based Document Embedding techniques, ultimately selecting the best performing features for the IR task. Our results indicate that a combination of traditional and Neural Network-based Document Embedding features yields the most accurate results. We discuss the advantages and limitations of our research, in addition to areas for future exploration. This research's code, data, and experiment descriptions are publicly available on GitHub. Abstract: This thesis delves into multiple areas of group theory, 
specifically exploring semi-direct products, Kummer groups, holomorphs, 
Cartier multiplicators, and their related properties. A key focus lies on 
understanding the relationships and characteristics of these groups when their 
defining series comprise cyclic factors. These investigations involve 
establishing the equivalences between the classes of group series, as well as 
their corresponding multipliers, and determining the implications on the 
groups' nilpotency classes, order, and associated homomorphs. These studies 
are carried out within the context of both finite and infinite groups.

This challenge has given rise to the use of unlabeled data in machine learning models, a concept that has shown significant success in various domains by leveraging the available unlimited data.  When applying active learning on these models, we observed that standard active learning methods select samples based on uncertainty, but often pick points that are easily identified and thus less informative.  To address this issue, we propose a framework that combines an underlying model utilizing unlabeled data and incorporates an active learning process guided by a query planner.  This planner prioritizes samples that, when labeled, have the greatest potential to improve the model's accuracy, as predicted by the model's uncertainty.  We evaluated our approach on K80 and A100 hardware using active learning on image and natural language processing tasks, resulting in a notable performance gain over baseline active learning methods.  Our findings demonstrate that guided active learning enhances public datasets to match supervision performance, also improving the convergence rate by 5-10x when employing unrealabeled data.  This approach also enhances private dataset accuracy by 10-20%, converging 2-5x faster than baseline active learning.  We open-source our code, models, and evaluation metrics for reproducibility. Our research addresses two scenarios: when the size of particles is comparable to the wavelength of light, described by GINISO, and when particles are much larger than the wavelength of light, described by KN. Additionally, we find that an increase in temperature has a modest effect on light scattering.  In contrast, changes in chemical potential have a more substantial effect, around 10-20, rather than the predicted 1-3.  These findings can be valuable in using light tomography to extract information about elliptical flow and fireball properties.  Our research also highlights the importance of distinguishing between longitudinal and lateral expansion in the case of elliptical particles.  It is noteworthy that the behavior of light scattering in heavy-ion collisions seems to be better captured by the KN model as opposed to the GINISO model.  Furthermore, our study suggests that future experiments with higher elliptical flow could serve as a more effective tool for testing the KN model, thereby gaining insights into the physics of collective motion in heavy-ion collisions.  In addition, our research indicates that collective motion studied through light tomography is independent of the medium's lifetime and thus supports the idea that collective motion in heavy-ion collisions is primarily an hydrodynamical phenomenon. Abstract: Accurate measurement of peak power in high-power laser systems is hindered by electrical measurement limitations. Our research investigates the interplay between laser cavity dynamics and photonic diagnostics, analyzing their impact on data contamination. By comparing photonic and electrical measurements, we have identified distinct system characteristics that influence artificial fluctuations. Our findings indicate that photonic data contamination can be minimized through appropriate probing techniques and by maintaining low optical bandwidth relative to cavity frequency. This knowledge enables the design of laser systems that incorporate photonic diagnostics, providing accurate data with minimal artificial fluctuations. Ultimately, this will enable more precise evaluation of the peak power achievable in laser systems. 

Presentation: The presentation will introduce the motivation behind our research, outlining the challenges associated with measuring peak power in high-power laser systems. A combined numerical and experimental approach was employed to investigate the complex interplay between laser cavity dynamics and photonic diagnostics. Key findings, including the minimizing of artificial fluctuations, will be discussed. Lastly, the implications of our research for the design of laser systems that incorporate photonic diagnostics are to be considered.

Consequences of this condition include an increased risk of falls, poor gait stability, and reduced mobility function. Current methods of gait analysis, which rely on visual evaluation and overall mobility measures, fall short in providing precise feedback for rehabilitation and locomotion training. Another limitation is the inability to account for the complex interplay between individual muscle groups that shape gait. To address these challenges, this research proposes a nonlinear muscle co-contraction control approach, combining empirical modal analysis and optimal control theory. A key aspect of this approach involves identifying optimal co-contraction patterns in muscle groups to stabilize and re-engineer gait. To achieve this, the model accommodates muscle co-contraction effects and incorporates balance dynamics to assess gait stability. Furthermore, the model is validated using healthy subject data and a case study is presented to illustrate its application to mobility impairments. Simulation results show that the proposed control approach can generate balanced and targeted gait patterns, while also providing insight into muscle co-contraction that may indicate spasticity. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a muscle-driven gait analysis that can inform rehabilitation strategies to improve mobility function.

Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a demyelinating disorder that severely impacts mobility and dexterity through unstable gait, reduced mobility, and an elevated risk of falls. Current gait analysis methods fail to provide precise feedback for rehabilitation and locomotion training, neglecting the intricate interplay between muscle groups that shape gait. This research introduces a nonlinear muscle co-contraction control approach combining empirical modal analysis and optimal control theory to stabilize and re-engineer gait. A key aspect of this approach involves identifying optimal co-contraction patterns in muscle groups to stabilize gait. In an effort to manage the spread of the disease, contact tracing has proven to be an efficient tool, but its success relies heavily on cooperation from the public. Although various tracing methods exist, probabilistic outcomes consistently compromise their accuracy, leading to unnecessary isolations and lost productivity. In an attempt to enhance contact tracing, we propose introducing incentives in the form of rewards for cooperative behavior, achieved through a combination of machine learning and evolutionary algorithms. Our simulation shows that in a population of agents, a proposed cooperative contact tracing system encourages collaboration, reduces unnecessary isolations, increases productivity, and locates the majority of infected individuals. The system's performance is further optimized when the ratio of machines to humans is higher, but this comes at an increased cost. Our findings also indicate that a softer revocation policy results in more productive agents and better detects infected individuals. The system's effectiveness is also demonstrated in an epidemiological model, showing that it reduces the spread of the disease and promotes cooperation. We apply the system to a real-world scenario, a university campus, and provide recommendations for its implementation. Finally, directions for further research are discussed. By conducting a statistical study of 109 young star clusters in three massive clusters ($Omega Cam, NGC 2079$, and the Large Magellanic Cloud's 'Bar' region), researchers found the mass function of low-mass star clusters to be consistent with the Salpeter or Chabrier power-law indices within a $1.0 \times 10^4 M_{\odot}$ mass limit.  No significant variations in the mass function of low-mass star clusters were found among the three environments, suggesting that the fundamental characteristics of low-mass star cluster formation have not been significantly altered by the massive cluster environment.  This finding is in line with the contention that the variation in high-mass cluster environment IMF profiles results from a top-heavy IMF in these environments rather than a bottom-heavy or flat low-mass IMF.  The study's results imply that the superimposed high-mass star cluster population is responsible for the top-heavy IMF profile in massive cluster environments, while the low-mass star cluster population remains unaffected and follows a power-law mass function.  This discovery highlights the distinct nature of the high- and low-mass star cluster populations and sheds light on the variations of the star cluster mass function.  It also underscores the necessity for further research into the formation and physical characteristics of low- and high-mass star clusters.  This study also expands the body of knowledge on the mass function of low-mass star clusters to below $1.0 \times 10^4 M_{\odot}$ in the Magellanic Clouds, a crucial step in understanding the overall mass function of these environments. Another instance is given by problems related to the scattering of light by

emission/absorption of light by moving quantum particles, specifically in a vacuum. 
According to quantum field theory, this phenomenon occurs at the same rate 
for all types of particles and is unaffected by their charge. 
A new proposal puts forward the idea of using moving atoms that emit a 
bluer light when in motion to a certain speed, in order to demonstrate a 
type of time dilation effect that could also be confirmed by measuring the 
frequency of emitted light from these atoms.

In the real domain, we establish the global-in-time existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified Klein-Gordon equation under mild initial conditions, and show that these solutions converge smoothly to zero as time approaches infinity. In the complex domain, we find that small, non-zero-residue solutions decay smoothly to zero as time runs out, while solutions with arbitrary residue values exhibit a more complex asymptotic behavior, encompassing both stable and unstable patterns of decay. These findings are demonstrated through a combination of Strachtyk's approach to real-valued decay, and the application of a modified Betorque-Levy estimate to complex-valued decay. Ultimately, our research provides valuable insights into the interplay between dispersion and the nonlinearity of the Klein-Gordon equation, revealing its capacity for stable, unstable, and semi-stable behavior over time. Additionally, our results highlight the significance of boundary conditions in influencing the equation's asymptotic behavior at infinity. Lastly, our research indicates that smooth decay to zero is a hallmark of stable solutions to weakly nonlinear wave equations. The general AL approach involves making queries from a reduced dataset, with a focus on obtaining new labeled data in order to enhance the accuracy of a model trained using a combination of labeled and unlabeled data.  In contrast, we propose a non-conventional Active Learning framework known as 'Predictive Data Reduction' (PDR), where the goal is to decrease the size of a dataset while maintaining or surpassing model performance, using only previously labeled data.  Our PDR algorithm, the 'Iterative Maximum Variance Reducer' (IMVR), is a non-interactive AL method that successiveley refines a reduced dataset, with the aim of maximizing the distance between data points that yield similar predictions.  Our experimental findings demonstrate IMVR's capability to achieve substantial data reductions (95%) while maintaining or improving model accuracy, when compared to conventional AL methods.  Our results also highlight the key advantage of PDR, which is its ability to leverage previously labeled data for smart reductions, thereby increasing its queries' effectiveness.  The implications of our research are that models can be effectively trained using a small initial labeled dataset, a phenomenon we term 'the AL warm-up effect'.  Our work offers a unique perspective on Active Learning, with the aim of inspiring research focused on exploring relationships between data reduction and label acquisition.  In particular, we investigate the concept that machines can learn more efficiently from humans in proportion to the reduction in data size induced by smart active learning.  Ultimately, our research may pave the way for overlying active learning on pre-trained models, a scenario where models are first reduced in size, with the aim of achieving human model comparisons on large datasets. This work presents a novel technique, called Real-Time Feature Extraction (RT-FE), which utilizes a combination of methods to selectively pass only the most critical information to the learning algorithm, thereby increasing both efficiency and accuracy. Our proposed RT-FE framework consists of three key components, each tailored to the characteristics of the sensor data from radar, camera, and lidar sensors. These components leverage techniques such as projection, classification, and clustering to compress the data. Ultimately, the RT-FE framework is an effective solution for enhancing the performance and resource utilization of an AD system, which can be applied to other safety-critical ML systems. However, the high cost of implementing optical communication, limited availability, and technical complexity of setting up optical links are significant barriers, especially in dynamic and ever-changing indoor environments. Fortunately, a relatively new field of research, Terahertz wireless communication, presents an exciting opportunity for high-speed indoor communication. Although there is limited research on THz wireless communication, it poses several technical challenges due to the extremely short duration of THz signals and the complexity of finding optimal transmission and reception locations. In response to these difficulties, we are introducing a novel method, Data Intensity Mapping (DIM), which utilizes data transmission power to determine optimal communication points. At its core, DIM employs machine learning to establish a correlation between transmission power and received signal intensity, allowing for the identification of suitable transmission and reception locations. We thoroughly analyze DIM's performance in two scenarios, one with THz communication and the other with conventional wireless communication, verifying its effectiveness and finding DIM to be highly efficient. Our results demonstrate DIM's capability to identify up to 75% of optimal communication points based on transmission power alone, with the remaining points requiring more complex signal processing, highlighting the substantial benefits of using transmission power as a simple and efficient solution. Notably, transmission power plays an even more significant role in THz communication, presenting tremendous opportunities for DIM to have a more substantial impact. We also provide concrete recommendations for implementing DIM, advising on the selection of transmission power levels and providing a clear roadmap for future research. Our proposed approach is highly versatile, applicable to a wide range of research scenarios and offering significant potential for future communication systems. One notable challenge in power system management involves handling load forecasts that are contaminated with high levels of noise, which can arise from unexpected events or inaccuracies in measurement tools. One crucial component of power system management involves forecasting future energy demands from households and businesses, also known as load forecasts. These predictions are essential for scheduling and pricing of energy, and they play a key role in preventing blackouts and minimizing the cost of generating energy. 

However, load forecasts are subject to significant errors due to various factors such as weather conditions, special events, and measurement tool inaccuracies, which can result in costly over or under production of energy. 

This research focuses on robust optimization of load forecasts that are contaminated with high levels of noise, which is an essential consideration for power system management in the future. 

To provide context, a brief overview of power system management, load forecasting, robust optimization, superarity, variational algorithms, big m method, and big K method will be presented. 

Then, an expression for the forecast error will be derived, and an explicit formulation for robust optimization will be presented.

et al. recently developed an algorithm to quickly identify toptal prime numbers, which are prime numbers whose prime factors are all greater than the square root of the number. This note explains their method in greater detail and suggests improvements to their approach. Their algorithm utilizes a prime number detection method based on number of digits, which we believe is not the most efficient way to find top-$k$ prime numbers. A combined use of sort-based and binary search-based methods would likely be more effective. We also propose a Top-$k$ Prime Number Detection problem and suggest a more general term of Super Prime Number Detection to encompass various top-$k$ prime number identification tasks. This note provides an introduction to investigating this problem through fast prime number detection methods. Finally, we outline the implications of our findings on the cost estimation of distributed algorithms that rely on communicating prime numbers.   Abstract
  The accuracy with which a model translates hand-drawn sketches
  back into real images is evaluated using a cognitive sciences
  framework. Two implicit neural network models, specifically
  StyleGAN and DALL-E, are tested with a set of sketches
  depicting everyday objects. One of the models successfully
  recaptures the original features of the target objects, even
  when the sketches are distorted. However, both models struggle
  with recovering the boundaries of the objects. The findings
  provide initial insights into a cognitive analysis of image
  translation. Code and additional details can be found at https://github.com/andersonwm/dabbing-sketch-real.

environment. The platform includes a range of user-friendly features, along with the

proofs into mathematics education, along with the potential for automated proof 
checking to enhance student learning experiences. The system's educational impact is 
further highlighted through our results from using the proof video in an undergraduate

To comprehend the pandemic's impact on employment, we explored the relationship between local virus prevalence and job market outcomes in the United States. Our analysis revealed a strong link between unemployment rates and COVID-19 case counts in major US cities. To further investigate this association, we leveraged employment data from over 17 million businesses spanning 1,100 industries, gathered from payroll processing systems for nearly 30 million workers. Our findings showed that as virus prevalence increased in a given city, there was a noticeable decline in average employment across local businesses, along with an increase in unemployment rates. Additionally, we discovered that industries linked to physical interactions and those within transportation and tourism sectors were particularly hard hit by increased virus prevalence. This review focuses on recent machine learning approaches to speech coding, a field where traditional techniques like linear prediction and Gaussian mixture models are being supplemented or replaced by alternatives.  We summarize three categories of ML-based speech coders: those utilizing neural network analysis by prediction and quantization, coders employing Gaussian mixture models in combination with K-means quantization, and coders integrating neural networks for analysis and Gaussian mixture models for modeling.  This discussion highlights the design elements, performance, and associated issues of these three categories, exemplified through Perceptual Linear Prediction (PLP) and Full Machine Learning (FML) speech coders. Given the rapid evolution of machine learning speech coders and the diverse evaluation protocols used, further research is needed in this area.  Ultimately, this review is intended to stimulate the development of high-performance, low-delay machine learning speech coders. This paper presents a novel algorithm to find all common subgraphs of size $k$ between two large graphs $G$ and $H$, rather than just identifying the largest common subgraph. Rather than applying traditional methods, our approach leverages a unique set of smaller common subgraphs. These subgraphs form a lattice, with each subgraph of size $k$ being part of a unique path from a subgraph of size $1$ to a subgraph of size $k$. Our solution first establishes these paths for any two graphs, then allows for efficient querying of all subgraphs of size $k$. This results in significant time improvements when compared to existing benchmark methods. Our algorithm demonstrates particularly impressive time gains for large graphs and large subgraphs, with query times reduced by up to $5$ orders of magnitude when compared to brute force methods. Our method's efficiency is also demonstrated through various graph types, including social graphs, citation graphs, and large scale web graphs. These results show our algorithm can identify all subgraphs of size $k$ in time that is near linear to the total graph data, with time gains of up to $10^5$ times better than brute force methods. This is achieved without sacrificing precision, with results matched against manual counting for small subgraphs, and validated against existing methods for larger subgraphs. Our research investigates this idea by exploring the concept of an all-encompassing defense function that consistently overcomes various types of attacks by consistently outperforming the attacker's strategy in terms of loss. We introduce the Generalized Loss Gap (GLG) as a unified metric to evaluate the efficacy of this defense function in relation to multiple types of attacks and their varying frequencies. Our proposed GLDF framework, Generalized Loss Distillation Framework, serves as a comprehensive loss distillation method that aims to minimize GLG. Our study also highlights the critical role of data frequency in designing effective defense strategies and provides a concrete roadmap for designers to choose loss distillation techniques based on data frequency. This paper proposes a new method for analyzing these types of systems by reversing the perspective of their standard state space representation. By inverting the signs of the state variables, we convert a standard system described by $\dot{x} = f(x)$ into one described by $\dot{x} = -f(x)$. Our main achievement is to establish the conditions under which this reversed system is stable, given that the original system is globally asymptotically stable. Additionally, we examine the implications of inverting the signs of the state variables on other system properties, such as its equilibrium points, flows, reachable sets and Lyapunov functions. Our findings are illustrated through numerical examples and their relevance discussed in the context of recent research on inverse systems. Ultimately, our goal is to encourage a broader exploration of the negative excess or deficiency framework in various fields of application. Our work is accompanied by a verified implementation available online. We have developed an experimental protocol to simulate a real-world attack on smart speakers, testing their security vulnerabilities when connected to a compromised Wi-Fi network. Our findings reveal that, using publicly available skills, it is possible to trigger a smart speaker to download an infected firmware by exploiting flaws in their security protocols. We first develop a method for accurate self-consistent field (SCF) solutions, then utilize an iterative RPA solver that incorporates an RPA correction to the two-body interaction, bypassing traditional summation techniques. In initial applications, we address the SCF problem for realistic nuclear systems and evaluate their RPA correlation energies using the JISP solver.  These systems comprise $^{39}$Mg with two-body forces and $^{40}$Mg with both two- and three-body forces.  Our results show that accurate SCF solutions are obtainable through our iterative RPA solver, yielding significant improvements in RPA correlation energies when compared to conventional solvers.  In particular, our analysis reveals that our method is capable of bypassing the failure to attain exact eigenvalues and eigenvectors in the RPA solution. Our simulations consider two types of magnetic field strengths, both in the disk's core and in its outer layers, and analyze their impact on the formation of gravitationally unstable regions in the disk. The models with strong magnetic fields in the disk's core and weak magnetic fields in its outer layers showed the greatest increase in the mass of gravitationally unstable regions; however, even with these variations, the mass of gravitationally unstable regions remained relatively stable at approximately 1% of the disk's total mass. Notably, the distribution of the mass of gravitationally unstable regions within the disk was unaffected by the magnetic field's strength. The models indicated that the mass of gravitationally unstable regions is primarily influenced by the disk's rotation curve and its density, and as such, it is largely determined by the disk's inner radius and the rate at which it accretes matter. The increase in the mass of gravitationally unstable regions in our strong magnetic field models resulted in a greater accumulation of massive protoplanets, and as such, it is possible that the presence of strong magnetic fields could lead to the formation of massive planets and super-Earths. In contrast, the decrease in the mass of gravitationally unstable regions in our weak magnetic field models resulted in a greater accumulation of small, planetesimals-sized bodies, and as such, it is possible that the absence of strong magnetic fields could lead to the formation of small, rocky planets. As such, the development of gravitationally unstable regions within the disk has the greatest impact on the formation of planetary systems rather than the magnetic field's strength. We call this kind of software "bridging" software. This study aims to identify the challenges of developing such "bridging" software and the factors that influence its effectiveness.

  Methodology: We conducted an in-depth analysis of five notable platform cases, developing a framework to categorize the complexities of developing "bridging" software. These challenges can be grouped into three sectors: (1) technical obstacles, stemming from platform design limitations and the need for backward compatibility; (2) market-related hurdles, involving the cost of development and the risk of dependence on the platform; and (3) ecosystem governance issues, including the difficulty of coordinating multiple "bridging" software projects.

  Results: We tested our framework by applying it to five new case studies, thereby refining it into a more detailed "bridging" software development lifecycle model. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical foundation and practical tool for companies to consider when designing platforms that support extensible ecosystems. These ecosystems rely heavily on the effectiveness of the "bridging" software, which connects them to the underlying platform. By understanding the complexities involved in developing such "bridging" software, companies can better address the technical, market-related, and ecosystem-related factors that influence its success. These considerations include the cost and difficulty of development, the risk of dependence on the platform, the need for backward compatibility, and the difficulty of coordinating multiple projects within the ecosystem. By taking these factors into account, companies can create more effective "bridging" software, which in turn will help them to build successful ecosystems and achieve greater success in the long run. of Private Learning with Persistent Adversaries. Unlike one-time adversaries, an always-on adversary has unlimited access to information about a learner's queries and data. We introduce new concepts, including the worst-case scenario in which the adversary knows everything about the learner's entire dataset, as well as the notion of average-case complexity which takes into account the variety of a learner's data set. Our study focuses on binary classification and analyzes the private learning rules proposed by Kearns, Shmoys, and Walkerdine (2020) which can withstand persistent adversaries of both the worst-case and average-case varieties. Additionally, we establish upper and lower bounds on the average-case and worst-case scenario query complexities for binary classification. Our findings demonstrate that upper bounds on average-case query complexity are directly related to the data set diversity, and that worst-case scenario query complexity is directly related to the data set diversity as well as the binary classification margin. Lastly, we apply our framework to private learning with persistent adversaries within low-degree graphs. Our research reveals that rule-based learning can achieve linear learning rates and that there are connections between the average-case scenario and the learning rates obtained through smooth loss minimization. Finally, we establish a lower bound on the average-case scenario query complexity which further highlights the benefits of diverse data sets in withstanding persistent adversaries. Overall, our research aims to illuminate the risks associated with persistent adversaries in Private Learning. AI-based models that detect hate speech rely on labeled datasets for training, but these datasets are expensive and time-consuming to create.  Active learning offers a solution to reduce the cost of labeling by selectively asking human labelers to label the most informative samples from the remaining unlabeled dataset.  However, standard active learning methods that prioritize highly uncertain samples do not take into account the differences in difficulty of labeling different samples, such as those based on the length of the text and the number of speakers.  We propose a new method that learns the representation of speaker and session embeddings, leading to improved performance. with research focusing on classifying visual stimuli to predict real-world 
outcomes.  Recent research using neural networks has achieved remarkable success in 
visual classification tasks, particularly when trained on vast image datasets. 
  We designed an innovative experiment to investigate how these classifications 
affect human behavior, assigning 1000 participants to complete various tasks 
while being presented with visually confusing images, and having them rate their 
own trust in these classifications. 
  Our findings revealed that when the classification is trusted, it significantly 
influences decisions in subsequent tasks; however, when trust is low, the 
classification has a minimal effect on decisions. 
  Additionally, we discovered that the perceived accuracy of the classification, 
rather than its actual truth, is what shapes behavior in subsequent tasks. 
  Our research implies that the apparent efficacy of deep learning in real-world 
tasks may be an artifact of participants' tendency to conform to the network's 
classifications, rather than a genuine reflection of the network's 
representational capabilities. 
  We propose a novel framework for assessing the true effectiveness of such 
networks in shaping behavior in response to visual stimuli, and our research 
offers several promising avenues for further exploration. 
  We also highlight the critical importance of considering both the positive 
and negative consequences of relying on these classifications in real-world 
applications, and the necessity of adopting a more critical approach to the 
evaluation of such systems. 
  Ultimately, our study underscores the significance of human behavior in the 
design and development of computer systems, and the need for a more collaborative 
approach that takes into account the potential interplay between humans and the 
technology they use.

$\mathcal{W}$-algebras associated with higher spin currents and their connection 
to Gelfand-Dickey integrable systems. Here we establish the link between these 
$\mathcal{W}$-algebras and classical bihamiltonian structures, demonstrating 
that they are part of a more comprehensive framework that encompasses both 
$\mathcal{W}$-algebras and superVirashoro algebras. This framework is 
characterized by weighted quadratic Hamiltonians that generate weighted 
semi-direct extensions of the Heisenberg algebras. By adjusting the weights, 
this framework can yield both $\mathcal{W}$-algebras with spin $s\geq 3$ and 
superVirashoro algebras. Furthermore, our investigation discloses an 
unprecedented bihamiltonian structure associated with $\mathcal{W}_3$ algebra, 
which arises when the spin $s=3$ and the fundamental Poisson bracket is 
modified using a Casimir function. This modified bihamiltonian structure 
leads to a 4-Poisson tensor that is in accord with the one reported in 
[9]. Moreover, our study reveals that both the classical and algebraic 
$\mathcal{W}_4$ algebras are fueled by repeated applications of the 
Bäcklund transformation, which amounts to successive integrable deformations 
of the base Heisenberg algebras. This finding holds significance as it 
confirms that $\mathcal{W}_4$ algebra is an infinite sequence rather than a 
finite set of algebras. Our research employs two methods: the first involves 
the extension of the Gelfand-Dickey scheme to soliton algebras of higher 
spin currents, which yields $\mathcal{W}_3$ and $\mathcal{W}_4$ algebras as 
determinant fractional powers; the second method utilizes the Gelfand-Dickey 
scheme combined with the Drinfeld-Sokolov reduction formula to obtain the 
same $\mathcal{W}_3$ and $\mathcal{W}_4$ algebras, which can be realized 
through the repeated application of the Bäcklund transformation to the 
base Heisenberg algebra. Lastly, our investigation demonstrates that both 
methods yield the same weighted superVirashoro $\mathcal{W}_n$ algebras for 
$n=3$ and $4$.

Our research combines aspects of systemic functional grammar and theory of lexicogrammar with categorial grammar to develop a context-free generating system for the syntactic elements of language. We define the theory of lexicogrammar as a set of ordered associations between words and grammatical structures, represented by labeled trees. We then establish that any context-free language can be expressed using a system of coupled, context-free grammars. By applying the same methodology to the theory of lexicogrammer, we can generate the syntactic elements of languages like English. Our system consists of multiple categorial grammars, each corresponding to a particular word's meaning and structure. We demonstrate that this system meets the requirements of both the Theory of Lexicogrammer and categorial grammar. Our system's components, including its means-for-linking and theory-of-lexicogrammer, are presented as coupled, context-free grammars. We then show that this approach allows us to derive the fundamental properties of languages like English. Our method provides a general framework that can be applied to the syntactic elements of any language. Our system's ability to capture the essential features of languages like English is also demonstrated. We conclude that this combination of systems offers a comprehensive model for the syntactic elements of languages, and that it does so without relying on specific assumptions about the structure of sentences. Our system's capacity to express the syntactic elements of languages like English is demonstrated. We suggest that this system may have practical applications in areas like Natural Language Processing. Our system's theoretical foundations are rooted in multiple established theories of grammar. We believe that further research could explore the connection between this system and other aspects of language, such as its semantic and phonological properties. Our system's source code is available online. We anticipate that this work will stimulate new developments in the field of Formal Language Theory. the Western Corridor of the North American Power Grid has been lacking, which is surprising considering the significance of grid resilience. To address this knowledge gap, an updated and detailed representation of the Western Corridor, which is the high-voltage transmission network connecting the Western and Eastern grids in North America, is provided in this paper. The authors offer a simplified and bi-directional model of the corridor, which has been subject to peer review and validation using actual grid data from entities such as grid operators, transmission system operators, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. A preceding study published in 2019 offered an initial representation of the corridor, yet it was restricted and lacked the level of detail provided here. In contrast, our current research builds upon that foundation and makes several key contributions, which include identifying under-specified transmission paths, refining the capacity of individual lines, and incorporating bidirectional flow into the model. By providing a precise and detailed representation of the Western Corridor, our research can serve as a foundation for future research and policy applications related to grid resilience, which involve evaluating the impact of outages, assessing the effectiveness of redundancy, and analyzing the consequences of component failures. Furthermore, our work may also be applicable to other interconnected transmission networks. A subgraph of a graph $G$ is a quasi-minimal subgraph when it contains all $K_3$ components of $G$, and is maximally planar. A new technique is presented to solve the recognition problem for a subgraph being quasi-minimal in a graph that has a fixed maximal subgraph. This technique involves a new graph transformation called the 'unrolling operation'. The unrolling operation on a subgraph $H$ yields a graph $G$, and $H$ is a quasi-minimal subgraph of some graph if and only if $G$ contains a copy of $H$. Additionally, it is shown how to apply unrolling recursively to obtain a graph $G_i$ from a subgraph $H_i$, and this allows a time bound of O(~n^3~) for the quasi-minimal recognition problem. The unrolling operation is then analyzed to show it preserves a new type of graph structure called'shell-and-core'. When a graph G contains a copy of a subgraph H that has a specific shell-and-core structure, and H is a quasi-minimal subgraph, then G also contains a quasi-minimal subgraph. Furthermore, a new graph structure called 'core-quasi-planar' is defined and it has the same recognition complexity as quasi-minimal recognition. A new algorithm is presented that can resolve the quasi-minimal recognition problem in a graph G, given that it contains a core-quasi-planar subgraph. This involves applying the unrolling operation in a recursive manner. The new algorithm establishes that quasi-minimal recognition is decidable in a graph G, provided it contains a core-quasi-planar subgraph. The unrolling operation is an essential component for the new algorithm, and it is shown that quasi-minimal recognition is not possible through a generalised unrolling operation. A new graph parameter called the unrolling number is defined and it demonstrates that quasi-minimal recognition can be solved by a parameterised algorithm that uses unrollings as a parameter. The unrolling number has an expressive definition and it is equivalent to a sum of parameters that relate to graph decompositions. A new algorithm is presented that can resolve the quasi-minimal recognition problem in a graph G, given that it contains a subgraph with a specific structure and the unrolling number of this subgraph is bounded.

Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the implicit framework through the lens of dynamical systems, which has the potential to guide future innovations in deep learning.   Introduction \\ 
  -------------

  This Python module provides a simplified rotation curve model that can be utilized for data fitting. It is designed to be compatible with the `GalPy` framework. The code is structured to enable easy extension of the model, making it suitable for complex data analysis. The module includes sample usage examples and tests. The code is documented with docstrings and includes a demonstration of how to employ `scipy.optimize` functions for data fitting. 

  Installation \\ 
  -------------

  To install the package, execute the following command within your terminal: 
  ```bash
  pip install git+https://github.com/jsersner/GalRotpy.git@main#egg=GalRotpy
  ```

  Usage \\ 
  -------

  For further information on how to use the module, consult the API documentation available at: 
  https://jsersner.github.io/GalRotpy/api.html \\ 

  Change Log \\ 
  -------------

  * Version 1.0 (2023-02-20): Initial public release of the package. 

  Rotation Curve Model \\ 
  --------------------

  The rotation curve model employed by this module is based on the simplified formula: 
  \[
  v_c(l) = v_0 + a_1 \cdot \left( \frac{l_0}{l} \right)^{a_2}
  \]
  Where $v_c(l)$ represents the predicted rotation curve value at position $l$, and $v_0$, $a_1$, $l_0$, and $a_2$ are model parameters. 

  Fitting Rotation Curves \\ 
  ------------------------

  To fit rotation curves, the module provides the `fit_rotation_curve` function. This function accepts a rotation curve object, a set of initial parameter values, and utilizes `scipy.optimize.leastsq` to find the optimal parameter settings.

Our proof builds upon work by Geometric Invariant Theory and the concept of a Baur-Bertrand graph. 

  Specifically, we demonstrate that $X$ can be broken down into a limited number of open, unionable subsets, combined with the connectivity of a finite graph to prove that its vertex set represents a subset of $X$'s point set, and finally, we show that this point set is then connected to show that $X$ is connected. 

  Within this proof, we introduce the term 'weak connectivity,' which means that a finite set of geometric points on a variety can be connected to show that its point set is connected. 

  We also show that any smooth projective surface $X$ is trigonally connected, which means that any set of three geometric points on $X$ is enough to connect the point set of $X$.

  We also provide an alternative proof of countably finite Hilbert's Satz using our proof of Kollman's theorem. 

  Finally, we demonstrate the connection between our proof and the work of Artin and Mumford.

  We show that our proof of Kollman's theorem can be used to provide an alternative proof of weak Artin-Serre's conjecture.

Tree was recently introduced to build upon the basic concept of a Phylogeny Tree. This new tree structure includes additional information, mapping, which indicates the geographical origin of each species present in the tree. A key requirement for a Phylogeny Tree is the Ultrametric Property, which the Persistent Phylogeny Tree must satisfy. Now, a new algorithm is proposed to construct a Persistent Phylogeny Tree meeting this criterion from a set of labeled metric trees, without a common ancestor. This algorithm results in a tree with the desired Ultrametric Property and can be seen as a generalization of the Hennig's Trio. Furthermore, it is proven that constructing a Persistent Phylogeny Tree is possible in O(n^2) time for n species and the challenge remains to efficiently determine if a given tree can be transformed into an Ultrametric tree. The proposed algorithm also includes a new method to estimate the minimum height of a metric tree, which can be used to optimize the construction of a Persistent Phylogeny Tree. This new approach to phylogeny trees paves the way for future research to address open questions and might find applications in Geographic Range Evolution Inference. Finally, the proposed algorithm has been implemented and is available for public use. This work is the result of a research collaboration conducted while the author was an intern at Microsoft Research. By formulating a mathematical function based on optical observations, the unknown three-dimensional meteor path is calculated. Expected feature importance is equivalent to conditioning on the data's conditional distribution, whereas variance-based feature importance instead assesses how much each feature contributes to the variation in the data used to train the model.  Our research focuses on a diverse range of machine learning models and real-world datasets, comparing feature importance metrics including expected and variance-based approaches.  We found variance-based feature importance to be more robust in many situations, outperforming expected feature importance in our experiments.  A theoretical justification for these results is provided by relating feature importance to the data's conditional distribution and its underlying structure.  We also developed an iterative tree-scoring function that improves current methods for computing variance-based feature importance.  Our approach involves multiplying the scores of each node's child nodes by the conditional variance of the parent node's feature, providing an intuitive explanation for how variance-based feature importance works.  These results can guide practitioners in choosing feature importance metrics and implementing variance-based feature importance efficiently. While previous work successfully demonstrated the feasibility of using collaborative filtering and knowledge graphs to predict student knowledge, this study aims to explore alternative approaches. We experimented with supervised learning, decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks to analyze their effectiveness. Our findings reveal that neural networks yield the most impressive results, achieving an average explanation score of 2.47 across 11 courses and explaining 41% of student errors. Furthermore, we observed that models trained on aggregated student data fail to capture individual student knowledge, underscoring the importance of incorporating unique student features. Additionally, our research highlights variations in the performance of these models across different courses and identifies patterns in data density and model performance. We believe that this work contributes valuable insights to the educational field, with implications for the development of intelligent learning systems that provide personalized feedback. These systems are crucial for addressing the challenge of providing individualized instruction to large cohorts of students. We encourage researchers and educators to explore knowledge graph construction and the evaluation of explanatory models in the educational setting. mathsf{GF}}(2)[x]$ is considered'skew' if its degree is odd, denoted as $d(f) = 2k-1$. This note explores the concept of skew polynomials and their associated binary quadratic skew extensions. Specifically, if a skew polynomial $f(x)$ satisfies the condition that its constant term is one, i.e., $\delta(f) = 1$, this note investigates the properties of the corresponding binary quadratic skew extension $K = {\mathsf{GF}}(2)[x]/\langle f(x) \rangle$. Although $K$ may be infinite, $K$ is necessarily finite when it has a nilpotent element or when its skew polynomial $f(x)$ has a specific structure. Moreover, this note provides counterexamples to show that neither the nilpotency of $K$ nor the structure of $f(x)$ is sufficient to guarantee that $K$ is finite. Additionally, this note offers criteria under which two binary quadratic skew extensions are isomorphic, and it presents an alternative approach to studying the finiteness of $K$. Ultimately, this study aims to deepen understanding of the complex binary skew extensions and provide valuable insights for further research. 

Keywords: Binary quadratic skew extensions, finite fields, nilpotent fields, skew polynomials.

This research focuses on the genotype-to-phenotype mapping associated with planar graphs, specifically targeting the implied effects of edge removal on the connectedness of the resulting network. By representing the Parzen window density of node proximities as a binary string, we seek to optimize the mapping from edge declarations in a graph $G$ to the binary string representing the proximities of the nodes in $G$. This string representation is equivalent to the binary string associated with the proximities of the nodes in the graph $G'$ that results from removing an edge from $G$. We prove that this mapping is tractable for the case of proximities that can be expressed as rational numbers and demonstrate the computational intractability of this mapping for certain continuous proximities, such as the distanceto-nearest-$k$-point, when $k$ is less than the degree of the graph. Furthermore, we show that there are no polynomial-time approximation schemes for computing the minimum edge removal that makes a given node proximality change explicit, except for the case of proximities that can be expressed as rational numbers. We also introduce a heuristic algorithm based on local search for the edge removal problem and evaluate its performance on random graphs. This research provides initial insights into the properties of the genotype-to-phenotype mapping associated with planar graphs and suggests directions for future research. Finally, we make our code available for reproducibility purposes. Furthermore, we establish that such sets are infinite in number when the number of variables is two or more.  The identity equations in question are of the form t(x_1,...,x_n) = x_1, where t is a term built from n variables and the operation symbol f.  The free algebra A(W) is generated by the words w(f), where f is the operation symbol.  The term t is said to be positive if it does not contain the left identity e, and we study the set of solutions to the equation t(w_1,...,w_n) = w_1.  The category of minimal right ideals in A(W) is equivalent to the category of Boolean algebras with a unary operation u, and we show that such ideals can be defined by first order identities.  We demonstrate that every positive term t defines a Boolean algebra with a unary operation u, and that this algebra is atomic and atomic subdirectly irreducible.  We also establish that the identity e is not contained in the image of the mapping defined by the term t.  We use these results to show that every solution to the equation t(x_1,...,x_n) = x_1 is an infinite set when n is two or more. To build a foundation for understanding these, we'll explore key aspects of elliptic curves, particularly their integration and associated analytic properties. We'll then delve into the current developments and related work, including the recent breakthroughs connecting modular forms to elliptic curves of specific characteristics. This paper introduces the Heavy-Tailed Extreme Quantile Regression (HTEQR) model, building upon the Extreme Value Theory, to analyze outcomes that are uncommon and significant.  HTEQR leverages the Generalized Linear Model and Extreme Value Theory to develop a quantile regression method that effectively handles the sudden changes associated with extreme events and the sparsity of such data. By combining the strengths of the Generalized Linear Model and Extreme Value Theory, HTEQR provides a novel solution for understanding the factors that influence extreme outcomes. Lagrange points are now an attractive location for space missions.  As such points lie in interplanetary environments, understanding their surroundings is crucial for assessing potential risks to spacecraft.  Our study focuses on gathering statistics of high-energy particle flux near L1 in solar activity cycles 23 and 24, utilizing magnetic field observations from the NASA L1 point spacecraft.  We calculated the 9-month moving averages of solar wind density, speed, dynamic pressure, and cross-area energy flux at L1 during the two cycles.  Comparing the data to solar activity indices, we identified speed and pressure to be more closely correlated with solar wind energy.  In both cycles, we observed an increase in energetic particles during solar wind density and pressure peaks, specifically in energy ranges 0.1-1 GeV, 1-10 GeV, and 10-50 GeV.  However, the most significant enhancement in energetic particles occurred in energy range 0.1-1 GeV.  The findings suggest an increase in multi-GeV particles in both cycles, albeit with less clarity, and highlight potential mission planning considerations, such as avoiding LPAs during solar wind density and pressure peaks.  Furthermore, our study reveals potential risks to near-L1 spacecraft from high-energy particles during increases in solar wind density and pressure, which may be induced by low-orbit debris eruptions and Earth's magnetosphere interactions with the sun.  Our research has implications for mission design, strategic spacecraft positioning, and L1 orbit re-entry policies during solar wind density and pressure surges.  Future work could involve gathering Earth's magnetosphere statistics to enhance understanding of potential L1 risks.  In addition, our results may be applicable to L2, as well as other solar observation locations in interplanetary space.  Ultimately, this study underscores the significance of incorporating particle flux statistics into the design and operation of near-L1 and near-Sun spacecraft, taking into account potential LAs induced by solar wind density and pressure peaks.  It also highlights the value of tracking real-time solar wind conditions to minimize LAs risks to these spacecraft, which are critical for the success of the sun's physics research.  The study's findings can be used to develop LAs risk assessment models, which in turn can contribute to the development of near-L1 and near-Sun spacecraft, as well as provide statistical data to support the development of the SPC's LAs risk management framework.   language and its corresponding framework based on Halide, tailored for dynamic 
  reconfigurability. CoreExpress allows programmers to express data-dependent 
  reconfigurations and enables automatic reoptimization of workloads for various 
  reconfigured architectures.

  100x faster runtime compared to sequential, non-autotuned performance. 
  We demonstrate the efficacy of CoreExpress by applying it to multiple real-world 
  applications, showcasing significant performance improvements resulting from its use. 
  Specifically, CoreExpress yields a 10-30x performance boost over traditional, 
  non-autotuned implementations and complements reconfigurable architecture designs. 
  Further, CoreExpress accelerates certain tasks on Axiom by over 100x when combined 
  with reconfigurations, a feat that cannot be achieved through traditional means. 
  Finally, we open-source the CoreExpress framework for further community exploration. 
  With CoreExpress, we also release a suite of performance benchmarks, along with the 
  coreexpress repository available at https://github.com/ucclabs/coreexpress.

Recent advancements in machine learning allow for the automatic suggestion of team members based
on new project requirements, taking into consideration past collaboration data. Our proposed
approach, known as CoderRec, is an collaborative recommendation framework that suggests a team
by prioritizing relevant past project features and leveraging cognitive architectures for personal
preference models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CoderRec by comparing its results to
those produced by the state-of-the-art WRM and BPR algorithms under various evaluation
criteria. Experimental results show that CoderRec consistently outperforms the baseline algorithms
in accuracy, diversity, and overall team performance. The study also highlights the importance
of user preference in team formation, demonstrating its enhanced consideration in CoderRec
through user preference models evaluation. Finally, we discuss the implications of our research
for addressing the challenge of software development team formation.  Team composition is a central factor in determining the success of software development teams.

These techniques use two separate neural networks to generate proposals and classify objects, which results in significant computational expenses and necessitates extensive training data.  Integrating the proposal network with the classification neural network addresses the proposal network's ineffectiveness and the classification network's inability to optimize proposal quality.  Fast R-CNN and Faster R-CNN mitigate this issue by refining proposals through a region proposal network called Fast R-CNN and Faster R-CNN, which are based on VGG-16 and VGG-16 with FPN respectively. The proposal network's ability to generate high-quality proposals for images at high resolutions poses a significant challenge.  This paper presents a meta-learning algorithm called Meta-RPN that leverages meta-learning to train the proposal network for a broad range of natural images.  The proposed Meta-RPN trains a proposal network on a small dataset of 5000 images from the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset, which enables the network to generate high-quality proposals for a wide range of natural images. When training on a small set of new data, how can we quickly learn to segment instances on new images, given that we already have a well-trained model for segmenting instances? This model, which we call the 'base model', should be from the same domain as the new data. To answer this question, we first identify two key issues. One is that the base model's feature extractor pulls similar images together, but also pulls very different images together, which hinders learning. The other is that purely pixel-based methods can't effectively utilize the information from the base model. To overcome these obstacles, we designed a new framework called FISSEG, which stands for Few-shot Instance Segmentation using a Strong Generator. This framework consists of two key components. One is a generator that refines the base model's output and helps the model to learn from the support set. The other is a scorer that scores the instances on the query set, using the generator's refined output as a starting point. Furthermore, we proposed two techniques. COVID-19 pandemic was announced in December 2019, numerous studies have been conducted to comprehend the virus's epidemiological characteristics, however, many of these studies have reached their conclusions too quickly, neglecting essential statistical principles. A thorough understanding of the pandemic's evolution necessitates reliable statistical data, which must be accompanied by statistical methods that are equally trustworthy. In this paper, we examine the distributions of reported cases, reviewing the distributions of reported cases in 185 countries, as well as the distributions of cases within 212 regions of Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. Our results reveal that in the majority of the areas examined, the distributions of reported cases adhere to the logarithmic series distribution, which has predictable implications for data variability. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the distributions of reported cases can be accurately modeled using this distribution, which in turn allows us to make more confident inferences about pandemic trends and predict future data patterns with greater certainty. 

  From a methodological perspective, our research highlights the significance of meticulously examining the statistical properties of data before drawing conclusions, which is particularly crucial in the face of data scarcity, where researchers may be tempted to lean on theoretical models. In essence, our study offers a roadmap for researchers and public health officials to conduct rigorous statistical analyses of COVID-19 data, which is equally applicable to other infectious disease data sets that might emerge in the future.

LCD) problem is an optimization task where we aim to discover the fewest number of hyperplanes that can cover a given set of support points, and in doing so, these hyperplanes define a region with minimum volume in a specified space. This region serves as the safest area for an LCD system, and it is the standard goal of the LCD problem. 
    However, in a dynamic environment where new data continuously emerges, there is a need to adapt the LCD strategy. This paper proposes an online LCD (OLCD) problem, which involves continuously updating the safe area in real-time by incorporating new support points and removing those that are no longer safe. 
    We introduce the Online Multi-Armed Bandit with Hyperplane Cover (OLMBHC) problem as a more manageable version of OLCD. This new problem involves maintaining a safe region represented by multiple hyperplanes in a high-dimensional space, and we aim to design an online algorithm for OLMBHC that achieves a sublinear regret bound compared to an offline optimal solution. 
    We also present a general approach for converting an offline algorithm into an online one, and using this approach, we develop the first online algorithm with a sublinear regret bound for OLMBHC. 
    Furthermore, we show that this approach can be applied to more complex scenarios, and specifically, we derive an online algorithm with a sublinear regret bound for OLMBHC with diverse arm covers. 
    We also investigate two practical scenarios: one where new support points emerge at random locations, and one with an adversarial attacker. 
    For the first scenario, we prove a nearly linear regret bound, and for the second scenario, we establish a sublinear regret bound. 
    We also propose two offline algorithms as performance benchmarks. 
    Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our online algorithm through experimental evaluations. 
    We believe that our work paves the way for further research on online learning with respect to the LCD problem. 
    Specifically, we propose several open questions related to OLCD, and we share a related dataset available for public use. 
    We observe a near-optimal performance of our online algorithm compared to an optimal offline solution, and we find that our algorithm is capable of handling a significant increase in the number of support points with a sublinear regret bound. 
    We also discover that our general approach for converting an offline algorithm into an online one is capable of producing an algorithm with a sublinear regret bound, and we find that this approach is capable of handling diverse arm covers.

methods for estimating the velocity field and error variance in Eulerian direct velocity reconstruction (DVR) across varying resolution levels.  DVR uses stochastic methods to directly reconstruct velocity fields from particle data, offering several key advantages over traditional methods for estimating velocity fields.  While traditional methods, such as Lagrangian interpolation, can yield accurate results in certain scenarios, they have significant limitations in other scenarios, such as when particles are sparsely distributed, turbulent mixing occurs, or observation scales differ substantially.  In contrast, DVR has been successfully applied to evaluate scalar dissipation fields observed at different scales, but further research is needed to fully understand its behavior across different turbulence regimes.  This paper provides a thorough examination of the DVR framework, including discussions on choosing parameters, analyzing output velocity fields, and scaling DVR results to match the resolution of the original simulation.  The findings presented in this paper can serve as a guide for future research and applications of DVR.  Additionally, a new algorithm is introduced for estimating the error variance that meets the requirements of being computationally efficient and outputting an accurate representation of the error variance across different scales, ultimately validating its effectiveness through testing on three separate simulations.  The results show that the proposed method precisely models the error variance at both high and low resolution levels, which is essential for informing future design decisions and scaling simulations.  The code developed in this research is freely available and can be accessed through the DYCOMS website.  Future work may involve exploring ways to enhance the DVR framework to accommodate simulations that incorporate phase interactions.  Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of more realistic and statistically robust design concepts that can accurately model the dispersion of particles in the atmosphere. One such scenario involves medical diagnosis, where a patient's knowledge graph, containing their diagnosis and treatment history, along with electronic health records, needs to be shared with multiple healthcare professionals.  This scenario presents a unique challenge: aggregating the decision-making process across these distributed graphs while ensuring that the outcome reflects a consensus among all involved parties. The C-GNN framework first incorporates a consensus-based aggregation method among the graphs to gather relevant information.  It then employs a weighted attention mechanism to determine the relevance of each graph's associated data.  Finally, the model leverages a weighted multi-graph attention network to combine the information from the distributed graphs.  The authors extensively evaluate the C-GNN framework on multiple real-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority over existing GNN-based methods.
